title: Anchorline Logistics - Private VPC discovery
summary: Discovery focused on Anchorline's private deployment requirements: multi-region presence (US East + EU West), strict egress controls, cross-account VPC peering limitations, KMS integration needs, and a 60-day pilot requested. Redwood AE+SE outlined Private (VPC) options, networking patterns, and next steps for a benchmark pilot.

Maya to propose benchmark runbook and sample dataset template
Customer to share CIDR ranges and security contact list

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 14:00 PT 
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM); Tom Ruiz (Anchorline CTO), Priya Singh (Platform Eng), Ethan Wu (Security Lead), Nina Park (Cloud Eng)

Summary (auto): Exploring Redwood Private (VPC) deployment; network patterns, peering, private endpoints; pilot and compliance requirements.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros? we'll go through your current infra and then Maya will do a deeper technical run-through.
[00:18] Tom (Anchorline): Sure, I'm Tom, CTO. We run most workloads in AWS, us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Lots of regionality for data residency and latency.
[00:32] Priya (Anchorline): Priya here, we own the platform infra. We're trying to figure out Private/VPC deployment patterns for an LLM inference provider. Security and no public egress is big for us.
[00:45] Alex: Got it. high level we can support Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. For private VPC deployments there are a few common network patterns: VPC peering cross-account, AWS PrivateLink (VPC endpoints), or customer-managed transit via TGW. We'll explore tradeoffs.
[01:12] Maya (Redwood SE): Hi all. to set expectations, Private means we bring in a customer-dedicated control plane and/or supply an appliance in your VPC depending on the option. We usually recommend either cross-account VPC peering or PrivateLink endpoints for secure control plane connectivity.
[01:36] Ethan (Anchorline): Quick question: we cannot have any public internet egress for inference requests, and logs must stay in our account. Is that doable?
[01:50] Maya: Yes, we have patterns where all traffic stays in your VPC; control plane calls can go over PrivateLink or peering. Audit logs and metrics can be pushed to an S3/CloudWatch in your account, and KMS keys remain customer-managed.
[02:10] Nina: Are there any special ports or NAT requirements? we have a strict firewall and minimal NAT gateways.
[02:22] Maya: Usually only a couple of outbound connections for control & metrics, but for a fully airgapped approach we can discuss an on-prem host or VPC-only setup. If you want no NAT, we can place the inference nodes in private subnets with endpoints to S3, ECR, and our control plane via PrivateLink—so no internet gateway/NAT required.
[02:45] Tom: Our security team will ask about key management. we use AWS KMS with external HSM for certain secrets. can Redwood integrate with customer KMS or HSM?
[02:58] Alex: Short answer yes. We support customer KMS for encryption-at-rest and can work with HSM-backed keys for signing. We'll need to scope the exact handshake—Maya will detail that.
[03:15] Maya: For model keys and audit logs we integrate with customer KMS. there may be an agent or an IAM role we ask you to create. sometimes those bits get mis-typed in docs so we'll send a checklist.
[03:31] Tom: Also region constraints: our EU workloads must remain in eu-west-1. we can't route EU data through us-east. how does Redwood handle multi-region?
[03:43] Maya: We can deploy inference clusters in multiple regions and bind customers to region-specific endpoints. Routing can be by policy; you can pin workloads to EU-only. for cross-region fallbacks we only do that if you allow it.
[04:00] Priya: latency is a concern. For our last provider, we saw latency spikes when KV cache warmed up. does Redwood do prefix caching or KV cache sharing?
[04:15] Maya: Our runtime supports KV cache and prefix caching. We also have options for pre-warming and smart batching to reduce cold-starts. sometimes the transcript in our internal docs calls it 'KV cash' so apologies for typos.
[04:32] Alex: To frame commercial options: Hosted is fastest but public; Dedicated gives you reserved capacity in our cloud with stronger isolation; Private is full VPC integration so networking and data custody live in your account. Most customers with strict egress pick Private.
[04:55] Ethan: Cost tradeoffs? Private usually requires reserved nodes?
[05:05] Alex: Private can be either reserved (we provision capacity for you) or a bring-your-own model. For reserved we do commit pricing. We'll model TCO for both.
[05:20] Tom: Ok good. let's dig into the networking specifics. who owns the IP addressing? we have limited CIDR ranges.
[05:33] Maya: There are two common approaches: cross-account peering where our subnets are in our managed account and you peer them into yours—this requires non-overlapping CIDRs. Or we deploy in your account (a private subnet we create via CloudFormation) which reduces CIDR collision risk but means we need write access to create resources.
[05:57] Nina: We won't allow Redwood to create subnets in our accounts without a security review. peering likely easier.
[06:08] Maya: With peering you do need to ensure non-overlap; we can also use an intermediate Transit Gateway (TGW) if you have one. PrivateLink avoids peering by exposing an endpoint service and you create an ENI in your VPC. The tradeoff is PrivateLink typically supports fewer ports and is managed.
[06:31] Priya: What about cross-account IAM and roles?
[06:37] Maya: We ask for an IAM role with limited trust for some operations, and a role for S3 write if you want logs to land in your bucket. All scoped down with least privilege.
[06:49] Tom: Any regulatory controls we should be aware of—like data residency proofs, audit logs?
[06:57] Alex: We provide audit logs and we can ship them to your CloudWatch/S3. SOC 2 compliance pack is available—Maya will attach the SOC2 & architecture docs.
[07:12] Ethan: Do you support SAML/SSO for the Console? We need SSO for our admin users.
[07:18] Alex: Yes SAML/SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. For Private deployments the Console can either be hosted in your account or we can federate to your IdP.
[07:30] Priya: Network egress control: we run strict egress allow-listing. can the nodes talk to ECR and S3 via VPC endpoints only?
[07:42] Maya: Yes, recommended is to create S3, ECR, and STS endpoints in your VPC. Our images can come from your private ECR or we can push images to a customer-managed account during onboarding.
[07:57] Tom: What about service mesh or sidecar patterns—do you require ISTIO or something?
[08:05] Maya: No requirement. The inference runtime is containerized and we manage networking at the instance level. If you have a service mesh, we can work through port configurations.
[08:16] Alex: Quick interjection: a common misunderstanding is thinking PrivateLink = full L7 routing control; it's more of a secure tunnel. For heavy throughput we often prefer peering/TGW.
[08:31] Nina: throughput limits—if we have spikes during peak shipping windows can the clusters autoscale?
[08:41] Maya: We support autoscaling policies. For Private, autoscale can be configured to spin up nodes in your account or we can pre-warm capacity. There's also burst capacity options. We'll show numbers in the TCO.
[08:59] Tom: We will want to run a benchmark using a realistic prompt set. can Redwood run a pilot inside our VPC?
[09:07] Maya: Absolutely. Typical pilot is 4 weeks: network setup, smoke test, benchmark run with sample dataset, and then a performance/quality review. We'll need a sample dataset, expected QPS, and latency SLOs.
[09:20] Priya: Onboarding time? how long to go prod?
[09:25] Alex: For Private it's usually 4-8 weeks depending on approvals. If network and CIDRs are pre-cleared, we can move faster.
[09:36] Ethan: About logging: can we avoid copying inference request payloads to Redwood-managed storage? we want logs to never leave our account.
[09:46] Maya: Yes, logs can be sent to your S3 bucket or CloudWatch with no retention in our system; we can support that model. Some customers also choose to mirror minimal telemetry to Redwood for alerts.
[10:00] Tom: Are there any gotchas with peering across accounts and route table asymmetry?
[10:08] Maya: Route tables are the main gotcha. If you peer, you need routes for the specific subnets. Also peering doesn't support transitive routing—if you use a TGW that changes options. We'll include a network checklist to avoid common issues.
[10:25] Alex: Also certs and mTLS: we can do mutual TLS for control plane comms if you require it.
[10:33] Ethan: HSM integration—how would that flow?
[10:37] Maya: We can integrate using external key references; typically there's an IAM role and CMK configured to allow the Redwood service principal to use the key for encryption operations while the key remains in your account, sometimes backed by CloudHSM. We'll need security to sign off on KMS policies.
[10:56] Priya: We'd like to avoid any changes that require an internet-facing ALB.
[11:02] Maya: Not necessary. We can use internal ALBs or NLBs, and PrivateLink if you prefer.
[11:10] Tom: Are there SLA differences for Private vs Dedicated?
[11:16] Alex: We usually offer SLA-backed uptime for Dedicated; for Private we can agree to contractual SLAs depending on the commit and whether we manage the infra or it's customer-managed. We'll include SLA options in the pricing doc.
[11:30] Nina: compliance: do you provide penetration test evidence or third-party attestations?
[11:36] Alex: Yes, SOC2 report, pen test summaries, and we can share network diagrams and our security posture documents under an NDA.
[11:47] Tom: Any known limitations with EU data centers, e.g., eu-west-1 support for certain GPU types?
[11:55] Maya: Some GPU families vary by region. We'll map recommended instance types per region; sometimes quantized models run fine on smaller hardware—Maya: we'll include a region capability matrix.
[12:10] Priya: For the pilot, we need a simple checklist: required IAM roles, CIDRs, endpoints, and a network diagram.
[12:18] Alex: We'll send a network checklist and a template network diagram.
[12:24] Maya: Also include a sample benchmark template: prompts, expected QPS, and metrics to capture (p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens).
[12:36] Tom: timeline again—if we start next week can we be done with the pilot in 4 weeks?
[12:42] Alex: If approvals move quickly, yes. We'll plan for kickoff the week of Mar 16 with a target finish mid-April.
[12:52] Ethan: One last thing—db access: some inference features need access to ephemeral embeddings store. those must be in our VPC.
[12:59] Maya: We can host caches in your account or in our managed account with encrypted links, but given your constraints, hosting caches in your VPC is straightforward.
[13:12] Tom: Ok great. what's the ask from us now?
[13:16] Alex: Share CIDRs, security contacts, desired SSO IdP metadata if you want federated Console, and target dataset for benchmarks. We'll send architecture docs and pricing.
[13:28] Priya: We'll need the security pack and a short checklist for the network team.
[13:34] Alex: We'll attach SOC2, architecture, and network checklist in an email.
[13:39] Jordan (CSM): I'll be on the follow-ups to coordinate the pilot and logistics.
[13:45] Tom: Thanks everyone.
[13:47] Maya: Quick note, I'll also include a short runbook for the benchmark and a spreadsheet template to capture latency and cost metrics.
[13:56] Alex: Recap of next steps: Alex send pricing + TCO, Maya send benchmark runbook and region matrix, customer to share CIDRs and security contacts. Schedule follow-up 03/11 for network diagram review.
[14:12] Ethan: Sounds good.
[14:15] Alex: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for 03/11.
